rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 6 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window without risking an excessively long low-strength run. This gives retention coverage across nearly the full solvent range while keeping enough gradient time to reveal where critical pairs sit.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the goal is to cut retention time aggressively while keeping the elution window centered on the observed peaks. The first run suggests compounds elute over roughly phi 0.18 to 0.68, so a narrower, shorter gradient at higher temperature should pull the last peak closer to 10 minutes without likely losing resolution.

We are very close to the optimum, with all pairs still above 1.5 and only a small time penalty. Push retention down one step further by shortening the gradient and increasing temperature, while keeping the same solvent window to test whether the critical early pair and pair 4/5 remain comfortably resolved.

The current method is nearly ideal, with only the first pair just under the 1.5 threshold; lowering phi0 should retain and spread that early pair more without materially affecting the already-fast last peak. Keeping tG and T fixed isolates the effect of the starting composition on the critical pair.

Now that full score has been reached, probe whether the method can be shortened further without dropping any pair below 1.5. Reducing tG by one step while keeping the successful phi window and temperature tests whether the separation still sits on the CRF plateau with a faster run.

The 6-minute gradient still gives full resolution with margin, so test one more shortening step to find the edge of the plateau. Keeping the same phi window and temperature directly measures whether slope compression now breaks the critical first pair.

At 4 minutes the only failing pair is the first one, so lower phi0 one step to give the earliest compounds more initial retention and separation while preserving the very short run. This tests whether the sub-1.5 early pair can be rescued without sacrificing the strong time advantage.

Lowering phi0 improved the critical first pair at 4 minutes, so push one more step to see if that pair can clear 1.5 while keeping the shortest gradient tested. This is the most direct remaining route to a faster full-score method than the 6-minute gradient.

The 4-minute runs show the first pair cannot be rescued enough by phi0 alone, so return to the successful 6-minute window and raise temperature one step to see if selectivity changes can preserve full resolution while shortening retention further. This targets a potentially faster full-score method than the current best without making the gradient steeper.

Temperature worsened the critical first pair, so keep 55 C and instead narrow the high-organic end one step to make the gradient shallower while maintaining a short run. This should improve the early-pair resolution at the same 6-minute length, while the last peak is already so early that a slightly lower phi1 is low risk.

The narrower 0.15-0.60 window improved the limiting pair at 6 minutes, so now test whether that gain is enough to sustain full resolution at a 4-minute gradient. This is the best remaining chance to beat the 6-minute full-score method by combining a shallower window with the shorter run.

The 4-minute run with phi1 0.60 missed full resolution by only 0.02 on the first pair, so lower phi0 one step to selectively strengthen early retention while keeping the successful shallower window. This is a focused attempt to convert the near-miss into a shorter full-score method.

Now that 4 minutes gives full score, try trimming phi1 one more step to make the gradient slightly shallower and potentially improve the marginal first pair while keeping all compounds comfortably before 10 minutes. The last peak is still early enough that reducing the upper end should remain safe.

With the 4-minute, 0.10-0.60 method at full score, the next step is to locate the true shortest viable gradient. Jumping to tG 2 directly tests whether the successful solvent window still preserves all pairs above 1.5 at the minimum allowed gradient time.

At 2 minutes the only failure is the first pair, so use the shallowest practical solvent window to maximize early-pair separation while keeping the minimum gradient time. Lowering both phi0 and phi1 should give the best chance of rescuing that pair at tG 2 without risking late elution beyond 10 minutes.

The shortest full-score method so far is 4 minutes at 55 C, and the limiting pair is still the first one, so drop temperature one step to test whether selectivity improves enough to add robustness without exceeding 10 minutes. This probes whether 50 C gives a better fully resolved 4-minute operating point than the current edge-case method.

At 50 C the 4-minute method has much more margin on the critical first pair, so raise phi0 one step to see if some of that excess early retention can be traded for a shorter overall elution window while staying fully resolved. This explores whether a slightly less retentive start gives a still-perfect but faster 4-minute method at the more favorable temperature.

The 4-minute, 50 C methods still have comfortable resolution margin, especially on the critical first pair, so raise phi0 another step to see if the run can be made slightly less retentive without dropping below full score. This efficiently tests the edge of the robust full-score region at the shortest successful gradient time.

The current 4-minute, 50 C method still has full score and the first pair remains above threshold, so increase phi0 one more step to see if retention can be reduced further while staying on the CRF plateau. This continues mapping the upper edge of the fastest successful method family.

Phi0 = 0.25 was too aggressive for the first pair, so keep the successful phi0 = 0.20 and lower phi1 one step to make the gradient shallower. This should increase resolution margin on the limiting pair while staying at the shortest proven full-score gradient time.

The 4-minute method at phi0 0.20, phi1 0.60 remains fully resolved with room to spare, so lower temperature one step to test whether selectivity for the critical first pair improves further while still keeping the last peak under 10 minutes. This may identify a more robust shortest full-score method than the 50 C condition.

Lower temperature improved the critical first-pair selectivity substantially at phi0 0.20, so retest the previously too-strong phi0 = 0.25 condition at 45 C. This checks whether the better selectivity at lower temperature can expand the fast full-score region to a less retentive start.

The 45 C condition restored full resolution even at phi0 0.25, with the first pair just above threshold, so test phi0 0.30 to find the upper boundary of the shortest full-score region. This is a direct edge-mapping experiment around the fastest successful method family.

Phi0 = 0.25 at 45 C is a full-score edge case, so increase phi1 one step to make the gradient slightly steeper and see whether the late peaks can be pulled earlier without losing the now-critical first-pair resolution. This tests for a faster outlet profile within the same shortest successful 4-minute framework.

The last run nearly gave the fastest perfect method but missed by 0.01 on the first pair, so lower phi0 one step to add a little early-pair retention while preserving the steeper 0.20-0.65 window that pulled the last peak down to 6.2 minutes. This is the highest-probability final shot at a fully resolved 4-minute method with the shortest overall elution profile tested.
